subject: Mathematics

learningObjectives: Use the token model to understand and visualize integer multiplication
Apply multiplication rules for all combinations of positive and negative integers
Recognize and extend patterns in integer multiplication sequences
Apply the commutative property: a × b = b × a
Apply the associative property: a × (b × c) = (a × b) × c
Apply the distributive property: a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c)
Solve real-world problems using integer multiplication
Understand the relationship between multiplication and division of integers

keyTerms.definition: The number that indicates how many times to multiply another number
The result obtained from multiplying two or more numbers
A visual representation using colored tokens (green for positive, red for negative)
One positive and one negative token that together equal zero
The order of numbers doesn't change the product: a × b = b × a
The grouping of numbers doesn't change the product: a × (b × c) = (a × b) × c
Multiplication distributes over addition: a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c)
The opposite of a number; for any integer a, its additive inverse is −a

learnModeActivities.title: Token Model for Multiplication
learnModeActivities.description: Understanding multiplication through placing and removing tokens
concepts: Positive × Positive: Place positive tokens multiple times
Positive × Negative: Place negative tokens multiple times
Negative × Positive: Remove positive tokens multiple times using zero pairs
Negative × Negative: Remove negative tokens multiple times using zero pairs

learnModeActivities.title: Patterns in Integer Multiplication
learnModeActivities.description: Discovering patterns when the multiplier changes

learnModeActivities.title: Multiplication Properties
learnModeActivities.description: Understanding commutative, associative, and distributive properties

practiceModeQuestions.question: If two numbers have a product of 24 and one is −6, what is the other number?
Which property states that a × b = b × a?
practiceModeQuestions.explanation: The commutative property allows swapping the order of numbers in multiplication.

practiceModeQuestions.question: If 123 × 456 = 56088, what is (−123) × 456?
practiceModeQuestions.explanation: Negative × Positive = Negative. The magnitude stays the same, but the sign changes.

practiceModeQuestions.question: What is (−1) × a equal to?
practiceModeQuestions.explanation: Multiplying by −1 gives the additive inverse of the number: (−1) × a = −a.

practiceModeQuestions.question: Calculate: (−2) × (−1) × (−5) × (−3)
practiceModeQuestions.explanation: (−2)×(−1)=2, 2×(−5)=−10, (−10)×(−3)=30. Even number of negatives gives positive.

practiceModeQuestions.question: What is the sign of the product of 5 negative integers?
practiceModeQuestions.explanation: Odd number of negative integers gives a negative product.

realWorldApplications.title: Exam Scoring System
realWorldApplications.description: Calculating test scores with positive marks for correct answers and negative marks for wrong answers
realWorldApplications.formula: Total Score = (Correct × Points per Correct) + (Wrong × Points per Wrong)

realWorldApplications.title: Mining Elevator
realWorldApplications.description: Tracking elevator position in a mining shaft with positive (above ground) and negative (below ground) positions
realWorldApplications.example: Descending at 3 m/min for 60 min: 60 × (−3) = −180 meters (180m below ground)

realWorldApplications.title: Temperature Patterns
realWorldApplications.description: Calculating temperature after hours of consistent change
realWorldApplications.example: Starting at 8°C, dropping 5°C per hour for 4 hours: 8 + (4×(−5)) = 8−20 = −12°C
realWorldApplications.formula: Final Temp = Starting Temp + (Hours × Rate of Change)

realWorldApplications.title: Stock Market Changes
realWorldApplications.description: Tracking cumulative stock price changes over multiple days
realWorldApplications.example: Stock drops ₹3 per day for 5 days: 5 × (−3) = −₹15 total loss
realWorldApplications.formula: Total Change = Days × Change per Day

realWorldApplications.title: Submarine Depth
realWorldApplications.description: Calculating depth below sea level during descent
realWorldApplications.example: Descending 50 meters per minute for 6 minutes: 6 × (−50) = −300 meters

realWorldApplications.title: Debt Accumulation
realWorldApplications.description: Calculating accumulated penalties or debt over time
realWorldApplications.example: ₹500 penalty per month for 3 months: 3 × (−500) = −₹1500 debt
realWorldApplications.formula: Total Debt = Months × Penalty per Month

criteria: Can explain multiplication using token model
Can apply all three properties correctly
Understands sign rules for all combinations
Can set up multiplication expressions for word problems
Can interpret negative results in context
Understands when to use multiplication vs. other operations

commonMistakes.mistake: Not adding enough zero pairs when removing tokens
commonMistakes.correction: Always add the exact number of zero pairs needed to perform the removal

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing when (−4) × 2 means removing vs. adding
commonMistakes.correction: Negative multiplier means remove; use token model to visualize

commonMistakes.mistake: Not seeing the constant pattern in sequences
commonMistakes.correction: Look for what changes consistently (increases or decreases by same amount)

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing positive and negative in real-world contexts
commonMistakes.correction: Establish clear conventions first (e.g., up=positive, down=negative, gain=positive, loss=negative)

commonMistakes.mistake: Losing track of signs with multiple negative factors
commonMistakes.correction: Count negative signs: even number = positive, odd number = negative
Zero property: multiplication by zero always gives zero

teachingNotes.learn: Emphasize the token model heavily in the beginning. Students often struggle with negative × negative = positive, so spend extra time on the zero pairs concept. Use physical tokens if possible.
teachingNotes.practice: Watch for sign errors. Many students will get the magnitude correct but the sign wrong. Encourage them to write out the rule they're using (e.g., 'neg × neg = pos') before calculating.
teachingNotes.realworld: Connect to students' experiences. The exam scoring resonates well with students. For elevator and temperature, emphasize the convention that down/decrease = negative.

accessibilityNotes: Token models can use different shapes instead of colors for color-blind students (circles for positive, squares for negative). All interactive elements have keyboard navigation. Text descriptions provided for all visual elements.
historicalContext: Brahmagupta (628 CE) was the first to articulate explicit rules for multiplication and division of positive and negative numbers in his work Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta, using concepts of 'fortune' (dhana) for positive and 'debt' (ṛṇa) for negative values.
